name: Professional laser hair removal

lead: Professional laser hair removal leaves skin smoother with far less regrowth on the face, neck, beard line and body. Users typically see regrowth cut by half or more over several visits.

A clinician passes a laser or intense pulsed light over the skin; the hair pigment absorbs the light and heats the follicle, damaging it. Wavelength and pulse length are matched to melanin while cooling protects the skin. Only follicles in the growth phase respond, which is why repeated sessions are needed. Under the FDA's definition, permanent means long-term reduction rather than total removal.

paras: Treatment is usually at least eight sessions spaced a few weeks apart, done in a clinic or medical spa. It shows best on dark hair and lighter skin; light, grey, red and fine hair respond poorly, and device choice matters for darker skin.

Short-term redness and swelling are common. More serious effects include burns, pigment changes, acne flares and infection, especially with the wrong device for the skin type. Rules for who may perform it vary by US state.

angle.text: Clinic lasers heat the pigment in hair so follicles are damaged and regrowth thins, typically by half or more over several visits. It gives smoother skin on the face, neck, beard line and body, and works best on dark hair and lighter skin.

lead: Professional laser hair removal is a clinic or medical-spa procedure in which pulses of laser or intense pulsed light heat the pigment in hair so that the follicle is damaged and regrowth is reduced. People use it to get smoother skin, a cleaner beard line and neckline, and less body or facial hair without ongoing shaving, waxing or plucking.[1]

The principle is described by Wikipedia as selective photothermolysis, with light of a chosen wavelength and pulse length absorbed by melanin in the hair while surrounding skin is largely spared. Under the FDA's definition the result is called permanent hair reduction, meaning a long-term stable reduction in the number of regrowing hairs rather than total removal.[1]

Beyond cosmetic grooming, it is used for razor-bump problems in people with coarse, curly facial hair and has been tested to reduce recurrence of pilonidal disease.[1][2] Studies compare alexandrite, diode, Nd:YAG and intense pulsed light devices, and a small number of home devices have also been cleared by the FDA.[1][3]
infobox: Alexandrite 755 nm, diode 810 nm, Nd:YAG 1064 nm, ruby 694 nm, IPL [1]
Commonly eight or more, spaced about 3 to 8 weeks apart [1]
FDA regulates devices; practitioner rules set by states [1]

paras: Typical areas include the face, neck, beard line, underarms, back, chest, legs and bikini area.[1] Men use it to define the neckline and cheek line of a beard or to reduce stubble, and Wikipedia notes that men's facial hair may need considerably more sessions.[1]

Lasers can treat pseudofolliculitis (razor bumps) in people with coarse, curly facial hair.[1] A 2024 randomised clinical trial tested laser epilation as an adjunct to standard care for preventing pilonidal disease recurrence in adolescents and young adults,[2] and laser hair removal has been used on forehead flaps in facial reconstruction.[4] The cause and treatment of unwanted hair in conditions such as idiopathic hirsutism is covered in endocrine literature.[5]

Light absorbed by melanin heats the follicle's stem cells, and success depends on delivering enough heat for long enough. Pulse width is described as the most important parameter, with fluence measured in joules per square centimetre and larger spot sizes penetrating deeper. Contact, cryogen or cold-air cooling protects the epidermis, permits higher fluence and reduces pain [1].
Lasers act mainly on follicles in the active growth phase, so several sessions are needed. Treated hairs usually shed over two to three weeks [1].

Wikipedia describes the underlying principle as selective photothermolysis: a wavelength and pulse duration are matched so that a target, here the melanin in the hair shaft, absorbs enough heat to disable the follicle's basal stem cells while neighbouring skin is not directly heated.[1] Spot sizes of roughly 3 to 18 millimetres are used, and larger spots reach deeper follicles.[1]

Three cooling approaches are described: contact cooling (reported as the most efficient), cryogen spray and forced cold air. Cooling lets clinicians use higher fluences and reduces pain and side effects.[1]

Because lasers act mainly on follicles in the growth phase, most people need at least eight treatments, spaced from three to eight weeks apart depending on the body area; men's facial hair may need considerably more.[1] Treated hairs usually shed over two to three weeks, and Wikipedia advises against pulling them out because this can cause infection and reduce effectiveness.[1]

The best-described responders are people with dark hair and light skin. Lasers work poorly on light, red, grey or white hair and on fine vellus hair.[1] For darker skin, Nd:YAG (1064 nm) and alexandrite devices are listed by Wikipedia as the wavelengths used, with the Nd:YAG reported to give some success on black hair in dark skin.[1] Touch-up sessions are often needed after the initial 3 to 8 treatments.[1]

Wikipedia lists ruby (694 nm, pale skin), alexandrite (755 nm, all skin types), pulsed diode array (810 nm, pale to medium skin), Nd:YAG (1064 nm, dark skin) and intense pulsed light (not strictly a laser, pale to medium skin). Argon lasers are no longer used [1]. The Nd:YAG with cooling has been used on dark skin by experienced practitioners, with some success [1].

The approach was tested experimentally for about 20 years before commercial release in 1995 to 1996.[1] R. Rox Anderson and Melanie Grossman found that a laser could selectively target melanin to partly damage follicle stem cells; the FDA cleared the approach in 1997, and a 1998 Massachusetts General Hospital article was among the first published descriptions.[1] A 2003 review in Facial Plastic Surgery gave early practitioners an overview of the technique.[6]

A 2006 review summarised by Wikipedia reported six-month hair reductions of about 69 percent for alexandrite, 72 percent for diode and 67 percent for IPL, with no significant short-term difference [1][3]. The same hair-removal article cites a 2006 Cochrane meta-analysis reporting about 50 percent reduction for up to six months with alexandrite and diode lasers and no evidence of reduction from IPL, Nd:YAG or ruby lasers [3]. An intrapatient trial cited in the laser article reported 52.7 percent reduction with IPL against 69.2 percent with diode laser at 12 months [1].

Results depend partly on operator skill and equipment. Light, red, grey, white and fine vellus hair respond poorly, and large areas often need touch-ups after an initial 3 to 8 treatments. Men's facial hair may need considerably more sessions [1]. Lasers can also treat pseudofolliculitis in people with coarse, curly facial hair [1].

A small pilot study examined wax epilation before long-pulsed alexandrite laser treatment,[7] and a randomised trial looked at diode laser hair reduction after IPL treatment.[8] A 2015 randomised controlled trial examined hair counts, thickness and colour during and after treatment with a low-fluence home-device laser.[9] Wikipedia notes that some patients see regrowth years after treatment.[1]

Wikipedia contrasts laser treatment with several other approaches. Shaving is temporary and can irritate skin; waxing lasts longer than shaving but is not permanent; and electrolysis, in use for over 135 years, can remove all hair in an area with proper technique and several sessions, and works on all hair colours.[1][3]

The same article cites a 2000 study of 12 patients in Ankara in which alexandrite laser was reported to be about 60 times faster, less painful and more reliable than galvanic electrolysis; Wikipedia notes that the study did not test modern thermolysis or blended methods.[1] Intense pulsed light is described as not a laser, although it is often labelled as one; it uses xenon flash lamps covering roughly 400 to 1200 nm.[1]

Common effects such as itching, pink skin, redness and swelling usually last two or three days. The most common serious effects are acne flare-ups and skin discoloration; burns, hypopigmentation, scabbing, purpura and infection also occur. Numbing creams used over large areas have caused serious harm and even death, and allergic reactions to gels, numbing agents or early shaving are possible [1].

A review of ocular injury in cosmetic facial laser treatments describes eye injury as a risk when lasers are used near the face, which is why protective eyewear is part of facial treatment.[10] Aftercare described by Wikipedia includes icing, avoiding plucking of shedding hairs and avoiding early shaving, which can cause reactions.[1]

The 2006 review cited by Wikipedia reported side effects in 9.5 percent of patients treated with alexandrite, 28.9 percent with diode and 15.3 percent with IPL.[1] Pain is expected during treatment; numbing creams are available but are not advised over large areas, and icing afterwards is described as helpful.[1] Changing the laser type or settings is described as a way to address unwanted pigment changes.[1]

In the US the FDA regulates the devices, there is no federal practitioner licence, and almost all states regulate for-hire services; Florida, for example, requires commercial use by a physician or supervised clinician. As of 2025 some diode devices have been cleared for over-the-counter sale, and rules abroad vary [1]. Wikipedia identifies two diode home devices, the Epilaser and the TRIA, as FDA-cleared for over-the-counter sale.[1]

Consumer devices designed for self-treatment are widely sold, and in Florida anyone may use an over-the-counter device but not to perform laser hair removal commercially.[1] Rules differ by country: some allow anyone to perform the procedure with an approved device, while others restrict it to doctors or supervised licensed staff.[1]

Comparative studies of lasers and IPL for hair reduction are summarised above.[1][3] A 2006 comparison found no significant short-term difference between alexandrite, diode and IPL, and an intrapatient randomised trial reported 69.2% reduction with diode versus 52.7% with IPL at 12 months.[1]

Registered trials have tested laser hair removal for pilonidal disease, including a completed 22-person study[11] and a 302-person study of unknown status;[12] the JAMA Surgery randomised trial (patients aged 11 to 21, 1-year follow-up, conducted 2017 to 2022) also examined laser epilation in pilonidal disease.[2] A prospective study of 15 and 26 patients with expanded forehead flaps compared alexandrite laser hair removal during versus after tissue expansion.[4] These concern medical conditions rather than cosmetic removal.

timeline.event: Laser hair removal becomes commercially available around 1995 to 1996 after about 20 years of experimental testing.[1]
The method is first applied after R. Rox Anderson and Melanie Grossman showed a laser could selectively target pigment to partly damage follicle stem cells.[1]
The FDA approves laser hair removal, later described as permanent hair reduction.[1]
A Massachusetts General Hospital group article is among the first published descriptions.[1]
A study of 12 patients in Ankara compares alexandrite laser with galvanic electrolysis.[1]
